title: A Spark, Thrown
author: copied out by Perran Loam, Listener of the Circle, and sold cheap on Lantern Row
body:
# A Spark, Thrown

*The first working every Sayer learns, and the last one most of them are any good at. Copied four times over because the Circle makes you write a new saying three times before you use it, and I lost count. — P.L.*

## Before anything

You are not commanding the air. There are no commands. You are attending to a thing very precisely, naming what it is, and saying it until it is more so than it was. If you have not got that, close the book; the rest is a recipe for burning your own sleeve.

## The attending

Find the heat that is already there. There is always some. In a cold room it is in your own hands; on a summer road it is in the road. Hold it the way you would hold a name you are about to call across a yard: the whole of it, ready, not yet let go.

## The saying

Two syllables, both short, the second one harder than you think it needs to be. The Circle writes them **ker-tan** and the Circle is wrong; it is nearer **k'tann**, and Sayer Ondrael says the reedfolk have it as one syllable and get more out of it than we do.

Say it three times to yourself. Then say it once, out loud, at the thing.

## What happens

The spark goes where you are looking, not where you are pointing. Learn the difference in a field. Everyone learns it in a field eventually; the ones who learn it in a barn are the reason there is an ordinance.

It will set light to what it lands on, and the burning goes on a little after the spark is done, which is the whole of its use in a fight.

---

*Note in the same hand, later and shakier: it is loud. That is not a fault of the working. Kindling is the loudest school because fire is the loudest thing a small voice can make, and if you wanted to be quiet you should have gone to the Undercroft, and they would have had you, and you would have hated it.*

title: For Being Surrounded
author: Sayer Orlaith Venn, of the Circle; written at Fernhold in the tenth year of walking that road
body:
# For Being Surrounded

*For Hew Arden, Callum Arden, Tam Dessick and the boy nobody would name for me. I learned your names afterwards. You ought to be on something.*

## The case for it

Nine years I walked the Briarwold road alone and nothing came out of the hedge. In the tenth year four men did, and they stood in a ring, and everything I knew was a working said forward.

This one is said outward. That is the whole of the difference and it took me a season to get.

## The attending

Do not choose a man. The moment you choose a man you are saying forward again and the other three walk in behind the sentence. Attend to the ring itself: the shape of it, the distance of it, the fact that it closes.

You are naming *the space you are standing in* and insisting it is hot.

## The saying

The same two syllables as the spark, but opened at the end and carried — **k'taaa-nnah** — and said on the out-breath with your arms down. Down. If your arms come up you will throw it and the throwing is not what we are doing.

Three times to yourself. Once aloud. Turn a little as you say it; not a spin, a lean.

## What to expect

It is not a strong saying. It stands where you are and it burns what is near and it is over in a few breaths.

It is a *loud* saying. The ring came apart because four men were suddenly standing in a fire that had no thrower, and men do not like that, and they went back into the hedge they came out of.

---

*There are nights when loud is the whole of what you need.*

title: The Long Insistence
author: a Vale prayer-book of unknown hand, annotated (without permission) by Sayer Aldith Sulion
body:
# A Prayer for a Fire That Will Not Catch

*Said over a wet hearth on the mornings when the house is cold and the baby is crying. Vale, old, no author. — The prayer is struck through in a firmer hand and the working is written round it.*

## The annotator's preface

I have crossed the prayer out and I want it understood why. The prayer works. That is the interesting part and nobody in this building will look at it.

Eighty years of Vale women saying the same forty words at a wet hearth, and the fire catches, and the Circle's position is that the fire was going to catch anyway. I have stood in nine kitchens with a glass and it was not going to catch anyway.

What they are doing, without a word of theory between them, is **insisting at length**. Not naming the fire. Naming the *moment*: this is the one, this is when it starts, now, and now, and still now.

## The working

It is long. There is no way to make it short and every Listener who tries comes back with a scorched cuff and a theory.

You attend to the thing you want burning — not its surface, its **middle** — and you say the old forty words with the hearth taken out of them and the thing put in. Then you go on saying them. The saying is the working. Stop early and you have a warm stone and a sore throat.

Count eight breaths. Most people stop at five and blame the book.

## What happens

It catches in the middle and comes outward, which is why it does not go out when it rains, and why you do not use it in a barn, and why I have had to write that twice now.

---

*A.S.: I am aware that this is a devotional object and that I have written in it. The Circle may have my resignation or my results. It has never yet taken the first.*

title: Under the Breath
author: unsigned; printed in the Undercroft, Tollmere, and left where it will be found
body:
# Under the Breath

*If you are reading this you have been robbed, or you are about to be, or you are a Tallyman and we would like you to know we can print.*

## What Hush is not

It is not silence and it is not cold. Everyone starts by trying to make cold and gets a headache.

Hush takes the **noise** out of a thing. Out of its footing, out of its hurry, out of the part of its blood that is shouting go. The cold is what is left over afterwards, the way a cleared room is cool. Chase the cold and you will get nothing for a year.

## The attending

Attend to how loud the thing is. Not the sound it makes — the loudness *of* it: the wanting, the quickness, the whole racket of a living thing being in a hurry.

Then you take a share of that away. Not all. Nobody takes all.

## The saying

Under the breath. That is not a manner of speaking; it is the instruction. The working will not go if you push it. A Sayer who shouts Hush gets a sore throat and a lot of attention, which is two failures.

It is one long syllable with the voice almost out of it. Three times under the breath, and then once more, still under the breath, at the thing.

## After

It goes slow and it goes cold and it stops being in such a hurry to reach you. That is all it does. It is enough more often than you would think.

---

*The last page of this pamphlet is blank. That is deliberate, and we consider it a joke, and we are aware of how it lands.*

title: A Room With Nowhere To Land
author: dictated by Half-Ell of the Undercroft to a scribe who was not told her name
body:
# A Room With Nowhere To Land

*Taken down as she said it. She would not let me tidy the sentences. — the scribe*

## She calls it the manners

Not Still Tongue. The manners. She says the Circle named it and the Circle names everything after what it does to the loser.

## What it does

A saying has to go somewhere. You attend to a thing, you name it, you say it until it is more so — and the saying goes out into the room and lands on the thing and the thing agrees.

Take the room away and the saying is only breath.

That is the working. You do not stop the mouth. Stopping a mouth is a knife's business and knives are cheaper than we are. You take the **room the words would have gone into**, and the mouth may say what it likes into it.

## The attending

Attend to the air between you and them. Sayers are bad at this; they have spent their lives attending to the thing at the far end and never once to the gap. Half-Ell says the gap is the trade.

## The saying

Flat. No shape to it at all. She says: *say it the way you would tell somebody the price of fish.* Any lift in the voice and the working takes the lift as a thing to land on, and lands on you.

Three times flat, to yourself. Once flat, at the gap.

## What she wanted written down

That a Sayer who has had it done to them is better company for a month afterwards, and that this is the most reliable thing anybody knows about Sayers.

---

*She made me say it back to her three times before she would let me go home. I am not a Sayer. It worked anyway, which I am still thinking about.*

title: The Slow Case
author: copied at the Sayers' Spire, nineteen hands, none of them named
body:
# The Slow Case

*Copied from a copy taken from a copy. Each scribe has added a line about the room. The Circle has never cut them.*

## The working

Hush said forward takes the noise out of one thing. Hush said **around** makes a case, slowly and quietly, that nothing here needs to be in such a hurry.

Most things agree. That is the part that surprises people. The world is full of things going faster than they wanted to and they will take an excuse.

## The attending

You are not attending to a creature. You are attending to the **pace of the place** — how fast everything in reach is currently being. It has a pace. Stand in a market and then stand in a chapel and you will feel it change under your ribs.

Name the pace. Then say it slower than it is.

## The saying

Long, low, and repeated on every out-breath until it takes. Do not hold your breath to make it longer; you will faint, and there is a list at the Spire.

Three times, then keep going. This one has no single moment of release. It settles in, the way an argument does.

## What it costs

You will be cold too. Everyone asks. Yes. The case is made about the place, and you are in the place, and the Circle has spent two hundred years trying to write yourself out of it and has produced nineteen cold scribes and no exemption.

---

*Scribe's line, the nineteenth: it is freezing in here. I have added a brazier to the inventory list and it has been struck out by somebody who signs only with a knot.*

title: Where You End
author: a Tollmere clerk's exercise book; the name on the flyleaf has been boxed in twice
body:
# Where You End

*Ruled for accounts. Used for this instead. The working runs down the money column, which I am told is improper and which has not stopped me.*

## The first Binding

Binding is short sentences about where things stop. That is all of it. Every fence, ward, snare and promise in the school is the same grammar with a different subject.

This one's subject is you.

## The attending

Here is the difficulty, and nobody warns you: most people do not know where they end. They think they end at the skin. They do not. They end wherever they have been told they end, and most of us have been told very carelessly.

So before you say anything, you have to **find the line**. Walk round yourself. Where does your arm's reach stop? Where does the room stop being yours? Attend to it until it is a definite thing and not a feeling.

## The saying

Three words, and the middle one is your own name, and the Circle charges forty marks to tell you that.

Say it three times to yourself, boxing the name in your mouth each time. Then say it once, plainly, aloud.

## What it does

For as long as it holds, the world argues with the sentence instead of with you. It is a poor sentence. It holds about as long as it takes somebody to finish arguing, which is usually long enough.

---

*Second entry, later, steadier hand: I have drawn the box again. It is better. A person who has said this once will say it better the second time, because the first time they found out how vague they had been about themselves, and they did not enjoy it, and they went and got definite.*

title: One Short Sentence
author: Hob Crellow, drover, of Tamwick; set for first-year Listeners since the Circle stopped laughing
body:
# One Short Sentence

*Thirty years turning cattle at gates. I am not a Sayer and this is not a Sayer's book and the Circle may take it or leave it.*

## What I worked out

A bullock going at a gate does not stop because you are loud. It stops because you knew where you wanted it to stop before you opened your mouth, and it could hear that you knew.

That is the useful half of Binding and the Spire teaches it last.

## Before you say anything

Pick the spot. An actual spot. Not "away from me" — a hand's width of ground you could put a stone on. If you cannot see the spot you are not going to get the sentence out with anything in it.

The Sayers call this attending. I call it knowing your own gate.

## The sentence

Short. It has to be short. A long sentence gives the thing somewhere to be while you finish it.

Say it three times at the spot, not at the beast. Then once aloud when the beast is a stride off — not before. Early is the commonest fault and it is the one that gets men hurt, because a sentence said early is a sentence the thing has already walked through.

## What it does

Nothing worth the name in the way of harm. It takes the next step away. Against a boar on a lane that is the difference between a story you tell and a story told about you.

---

*Note added at the Spire, in the Circle's hand: we were rude about this book for a decade. We were wrong. It is set for first-year Listeners and Master Crellow declines the fee every year with what I can only describe as enjoyment.*

title: Standing Orders for a Barrow, with the Keeper's Bond
author: Wardens of the Hearth, Wardens' Rest; issued to Roll-Wardens and expected back
body:
# Standing Orders for a Barrow

*Issued. Numbered. Signed for. If you are reading a copy that is not signed for, take it back.*

## Before the mouth

1. Two lanterns. Light the first outside.
2. Rope on the outside stone, not on a root.
3. Count the party aloud, by name, and have them answer. Names, not numbers; a number cannot tell you which one is missing.
4. **The Bond**, over whoever goes in first.
5. Light the second lantern inside the mouth, where the draught will show you.

## Four: the Bond

This is a Binding and it is written here as procedure because that is what it is. It is not a blessing and the Order may say what it likes about that.

You attend to the one going first — the whole of them, the way you would if you had to describe them to a stranger who was going to look for them. Then you name where *they* end, out loud, and you put your word on the line.

It is a promise in the grammatical sense. It holds until it is broken, and then it is only a thing somebody said, and then you are both in a barrow with a lantern.

Say it three times to yourself on the way down the road. Once aloud at the mouth. Not inside. Inside there is a draught and the draught takes the first word off it.

## After

Six. Do not name a Hearthstone you find below ground until you are above it again.

---

*Signed for by: — and then nine names, each struck through and rewritten, and a tenth line left empty with a small knot inked beside it.*

title: An Instruction to the Excitable
author: Hesta Wick, midwife, of Merrowby; the run paid for out of her husband's name-day money
body:
# An Instruction to the Excitable

*Printed cheap on purpose. I want one in every house in the Vale and I would rather have a thousand bad copies than nine good ones. — H.W.*

## First, the honest part

This will not save anybody.

It will buy you the quarter of an hour it takes to fetch somebody who can. I have spent that quarter of an hour twice and both times it was the whole of the difference, and I am not going to dress it up further than that.

## What Mending is

Mending does not close a wound. It reminds a body what shape it was in when it was last spoken of kindly, and the body, being vain, obliges.

This one is not even that. It is an **instruction**, issued firmly, to the parts of a person that have become excitable — the blood that is hurrying out, the gut that is in a state, the heart going like a bird in a bag.

## The saying

Say it the way you would tell somebody's frightened aunt to sit down. Not unkindly. Not gently either — gently is asking, and you are not asking. As though the sitting down were already agreed.

Three times to yourself while you get to them. Once aloud, with a hand on them if you can; the hand is not part of the working and it is part of the working.

## Then

Press the wound anyway. Fetch somebody. The saying is the quarter of an hour, not the answer.

---

## A poultice for after

Yarrow, bruised, two parts. Marsh-marigold leaf, one. Bind with clean linen and change it at dusk. This is the useful half of the book and I have put it second so you would read the other one.

title: The Body, Being Vain
author: a field copy of the Order's Mending; the hand is Sister Auvrey Tull's, of Pilgrim's Ash
body:
# The Body, Being Vain

*Two winters in the Cinderlea. Water to the spine and ash in the gutter of every page. I have written in the back board the names of the people I used it on. — A.T.*

## The doctrine, briefly

A wound is not a hole. A wound is a body that has stopped agreeing about its own shape.

Mending does not close anything. It reminds the body what shape it was in when it was last spoken of kindly, and the body, being vain, obliges. The Circle finds this formulation frivolous. The Circle has not knelt in ash.

## The attending

Attend to the person **before** the wound. The wound is loud and it will take all of your attention and give nothing back. What you want is the shape underneath: how they stand, how they carry the arm, what they looked like an hour ago when nothing was wrong.

If you did not see them an hour ago, ask them. Out loud. Make them describe themselves. It is not a delay; it is the working starting.

## The saying

Long and level, three times through under the breath, then once through aloud and slowly. It takes about as long as a short prayer and it is not one, whatever the Order prints.

## What it will and will not do

It closes. It clears out what has got into the blood — the bleeding, the poison, the crawling fever of a bad wound.

It does not answer for everything. It did not answer for eleven of the names in the back of this book and I have ruled a line through each of them so that nobody who picks this up thinks they have bought a certainty.

---

*There are more names above the lines than below them. I have counted often.*

title: You Have To Mean It
author: Bennick Cresswell, Sayer of the Candle; the eleventh fair copy and no two alike
body:
# You Have To Mean It

*This is the eleventh of these I have written out to give away and I am told they do not agree with one another. Good. Neither do I, year to year.*

## The working, which is four lines

I will give it to you now so that you stop looking for it while you read the rest.

It is A Kind Word said over somebody who is not you. Three times under the breath while you get to them, once aloud with their name in the middle of it if you know their name, and if you do not know their name then ask, and if they cannot answer then invent one and use it, and apologise later, and they will let you off.

That is the whole of the technique. Now the difficult part.

## The difficult part

The Candle account holds that a thing spoken of kindly holds together a little longer than it has any business doing, and that this is the whole of Mending and the rest is arrangement.

Which means the working does not go unless you mean it.

Not feel it. **Mean** it. You may be frightened, you may be sick of them, you may have spent the morning wishing they would fall in a ditch. Meaning it is not a warm feeling; it is a decision made in the presence of a stranger who is bleeding on you, that for the next four lines this person is worth the trouble.

## How to get there in a hurry

Say one true small thing about them first, aloud, before the working. *You've come a long way.* *That's a good coat.* Anything, so long as it is true.

I do not know why this helps. Sulion says it is nonsense and I have watched her do it.

---

*The Circle has twice voted to cut these pages and keep the four lines. Twice it has not quite managed it. I intend to be dead before the third vote.*

title: The Dog Nobody Owned
author: Sayer Ismay Ondrael; eleven accounts set in columns, with the working drawn out of the agreement
body:
# The Dog Nobody Owned

*Eleven villages. Eleven accounts of the same dog. Four years. — I.O.*

## The columns

Merrowby has it black. Tamwick has it brindled. Fernhold says it was a bitch and had one ear. In Gullhithe it belonged to a man who is named and who never existed, and in Isseva it is not a dog at all but they tell the same story about it.

The name is different in every column. I have set them side by side so that you can see for yourself that this does not matter.

## Why it does not matter

Calling does not make a thing. It asks the thing that is already in everybody's mouth to come.

What is in eleven villages' mouths is not a dog. It is the *agreement* about a dog: that it turned up, that it saw somebody home, that nobody fed it and it stayed anyway. Eleven names laid over one agreement, and the agreement is what answers.

Finding out why the names do not matter took me four years and is the only finding I have ever published that made anybody happy.

## The working

Attend to the agreement, not to any column. What everyone says the same.

The saying is the shortest in the school and the hardest to keep hold of: you are naming a thing that has no name, and the mouth keeps trying to give it one. Three times under the breath, refusing each time to supply the name. Then once aloud, still refusing.

Students who insist on calling it something get a very long silence and a headache.

## What comes

Something that has been spoken of that often does not need much asking. It stands where you point it, it fights, and when the saying runs down it lets go and there is nothing left on the ground.

---

*It is not your dog. It was never anybody's. That is the entire reason it comes.*

title: They Come Up Holding It
author: a grave-warden's register of a village the Roll no longer answers; the working is in a later hand
body:
# Register of Burials

*The village is not named here and I have not restored it. The register is a plain list and the working has been written in between the entries by somebody who came after. — the Circle's cataloguer*

## From the entries

**Aunsy Ferrel, thatcher.** Buried with her hook.

**Tam Ollow, who kept the sluice.** Buried with the key on him, the Council having agreed it.

**A boy of the Dessicks, no age given.** Buried with a whistle.

*And so on for four pages. The Vale buries its people with the tool of their work so that the ringing will know them by it. That is the custom and it is older than the Roll.*

## The working, written between the lines

A Calling said over that ground is only a reminder of the arrangement. You are not raising anybody. You are saying, out loud, over a piece of ground where an agreement was made: **the arrangement stands**.

Attend to the ground, not to the dead. The dead are not the loud thing here. The custom is the loud thing — eighty years of a village putting the right object in the right hands and meaning it.

Name the arrangement. Say it three times with your hand on the turf. Then say it once, standing, and step back, because they come up where they are and not where you would like them.

## What comes up

They come up holding the tool. All of them. The hook, the key, the whistle.

They are not pleased. They were not pleased before, either. Do not take it personally.

---

*Last line in the working hand, pressed hard enough to have gone through two leaves:*

*Do not do this near a house.*

title: Off the Roll
author: three sheets in a Warden's hand, sewn into a board cut from something older; six owners, each of whom added a line
body:
# Off the Roll

*A page of the Roll, copied entire, with one working laid over it like a gloss. Whoever did this committed a crime. Whoever burns it will commit a worse one. — first line on the board*

## The page

Thirty-one names, read aloud at Wardens' Rest on Tollday, and eight of them deep lines that nobody answers to any more. They are set out here exactly as the Roll sets them out, which is the point: it is the *reading* that is being copied, not the list.

## The gloss

This is the highest Calling and the shortest working in the five schools. Four syllables. A child could hold them.

You attend to the reading. Not to a person — to the fact of a name having been said aloud, on a fixed day, in a fixed place, by people who meant it, for a great many years.

Then you say the name. Off the Roll. Once under the breath, once at ordinary speaking, once as it is read at the Rest, which is loudly and slowly and with a pause after it for the answer.

Then you wait. The waiting is not a gap in the working. The waiting is the last part of it.

## What comes

Not the person. It is important that you know this before and not after.

What comes is the shape a thousand evenings of being spoken of left behind, wearing the lantern and the tabard, and it will stand where you point and go out when the saying runs down.

It does not know you. It does not know itself. It answers because it was called correctly, which is all it ever did.

---

## The owners' lines

*Give it to Aldis Renn. She will not want it and she is the right one.*

*Gave it to Renn. She wept and took it. Give it to whoever has stood a night at the Choir.*

*Passed to the Order and taken back off them within the year, no fault of theirs.*

*I have used it twice and I am quieter than I was. Do not use it twice.*

*Give it to a Warden. Only a Warden should carry the Roll, even a page of it, even a copy.*

*— and a sixth line left half-written, and the ink dried on the nib.*
